The belief: EF Core changes data through the change tracker, and only through it. To update or delete rows you query them, change or remove the entities, and call
. Anything else means dropping down to raw SQL.

It's how EF is taught, and for a long time it was true. Bulk operations only arrived in EF Core 7.0, so years of tutorials, answers and code reviews predate them. The tracked approach also feels efficient, because
batches its statements into a few round trips. And it really is the right tool when you're editing a handful of entities that a user loaded into a form.
SaveChanges needs every row in memory first
The tracked path brings every matching row to the client, materializes an entity for each, snapshots its values in the
, compares each entity with its snapshot when you save, and then sends one
per changed row. Batching groups those statements into fewer round trips, up to 42 per batch on SQL Server by default, but the database still runs each one separately.
In a test with EF Core 10 on SQL Server LocalDB, deactivating 40,000 of 50,000 customers this way took 954 commands: one
and 953 batches. It allocated about 310 MB and took between 1.4 and 2.3 seconds on a local database. On SQLite, which sent each
as its own command, the same job took 40,001 commands.
